etymology: Hebrew Kittiyyim, a plural gentilic first naming the men of Kition in Cyprus, then the western isles at large; rendered “Chittim” in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The name Kittim, or Chittim, stands in the table of nations among the sons of Javan: “And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim” (Gen 10:4). It names the far western coastlands — Cyprus first, and the isles and shores beyond it toward the setting sun. From those distant harbours the ships of Chittim sail into prophecy. Balaam, constrained to bless where he was hired to curse, lifted up his eyes to the latter days and saw them: “And ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur” (Num 24:24). Daniel beheld the same keels turned in judgment: “For the ships of Chittim shall come against him” (Dan 11:30). Here is the comfort of the doctrine of providence. The proud reckon by their armies and their walls, but the LORD holds the far ships in His hand, and He summons fleets from the edge of the map to break the boaster in His hour. No empire lies beyond His reach; the isles He has never forgotten. The distant coastland, which seems to fall outside the story of redemption, is a servant in the counsel of God, raised up and sent forth to accomplish the purpose settled before the world was. The uttermost parts obey Him. Let the saint who feels forgotten at the world’s far edge remember that the ships of Chittim answer to His word.
webster_summary: The western coastlands — Cyprus and the isles beyond (Gen 10:4); the far ships that afflict Asshur in Balaam’s oracle and come against the wilful king in Daniel, all held in the hand of God’s providence.

corruption_paragraphs: Kittim is a name on the map’s far western rim, and it stirs no modern quarrel. Its lesson is the reach of God’s dominion: the ships of Chittim, sailing from the edge of the known world, come and go at His bidding.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the universal providence of God over the nations. The heart that reckons only what it can see supposes the distant powers to be free agents; but the far isles are His servants, and the fleets of the coastlands accomplish the counsel settled before the foundation of the world. Let the proud tremble and the weary take heart, for the uttermost parts obey Him.

etymology: Hebrew 'Elishah, a son of Javan and the coastland named after him; the isles whence came the blue and purple dye that covered the ships of Tyre.
biblical_def: Elishah is set first among the sons of Javan: “And the sons of Javan; Elishah, and Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim” (Gen 10:4). The name passed from the man to the coastland, and the coastland enters Scripture as a supplier to the pride of Tyre. In Ezekiel’s lament over the great merchant city, the awnings that shaded her deck are traced to these distant shores: “Fine linen with broidered work from Egypt was that which thou spreadest forth to be thy sail; blue and purple from the isles of Elishah was that which covered thee” (Eze 27:7). Here is the whole world laid under tribute to clothe one proud city — Egyptian linen for her sail, the royal dyes of Elishah for her covering. Tyre gathered the finery of the nations and wore it like a queen, and reckoned herself secure in her splendour. Yet all this costly traffic could not save her; the ship so richly rigged went down into the midst of the seas. The isles of Elishah preach the vanity of riches that cannot ransom a soul. Purple is the colour of kings, but the merchandise of the coastlands buys no place in the kingdom of God. Only the blood of Christ, not the blue and purple of Elishah, covers the sinner and clothes him for the presence of the King. Lay not up treasure that the sea can swallow.

etymology: Hebrew Arvad, a small rocky island off the Phoenician coast; its men served as mariners and soldiers of Tyre. The people are called Arvadites in the table of nations.
biblical_def: Arvad was a fortress-island of the Phoenician shore, and in Ezekiel’s dirge over Tyre her sons appear twice, once at the oar and once upon the wall. As mariners they manned the great merchant ship: “The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots” (Eze 27:8). As warriors they crowned her defences: “The men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about…they have made thy beauty perfect” (Eze 27:11). Here was strength borrowed and glory hired — the seamanship of one people, the valour of another, gathered to make Tyre invincible in her own eyes. The shields hung upon her walls round about made her beauty perfect, and she trusted in the confederacy of the coastlands. Yet the men of Arvad went down with the city they guarded. The strength of allies perishes with the thing it defends; no borrowed valour outlives the object of its trust. This is the lesson written over every league of the nations: what a man leans upon in the day of wrath shall fall together with him. The LORD alone is the wall that does not crumble and the pilot that does not drown. Trust not in the men of Arvad upon the wall, but in the God who is a very present help; His salvation is walls and bulwarks that the sea cannot break.

The believer leans not on the men of Arvad but on the Rock; the salvation of God is a wall the raging sea cannot breach.

etymology: Hebrew Gebal, “boundary” or “mountain range”; the ancient Phoenician port the Greeks called Byblos, whose skilled men were the calkers of Tyre’s ships.
biblical_def: Gebal, the port the Greeks named Byblos, appears in Scripture with two faces — a craftsman for Tyre and a confederate against Israel. Ezekiel names her ancient and skilful men among the shipwrights of the great city: “The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers” (Eze 27:9). Their hands stopped the seams and made the merchant vessel sound, that she might carry the traffic of the world. Yet in the eighty-third Psalm Gebal is found in another company altogether, banded with Ammon and Amalek and the Philistines in the confederacy of Asaph’s prayer, the nations that took crafty counsel and said, Let us cut them off from being a nation. So the same coast that lent its craftsmen to Tyre lent its arms against the people of God. Here is a double lesson. The skill of the nations is real; their calkers made ships that sailed, their builders raised walls that stood. But skill is no shield against the God of Jacob, and confederacy is no defence. The wise men of Gebal could seal a ship against the sea, yet could not seal their alliance against the judgment of heaven. Every league that gathers against the LORD’s inheritance is broken as the eighty-third Psalm was answered. Let the church remember: the craftsmen and the confederacies of the earth are alike in His hand, and He who scattered the raging heathen keeps His own.

etymology: Hebrew Tadmor, the city of palms in the wilderness, the later Palmyra; built by Solomon as a store city far out in the desert land.
biblical_def: Tadmor was Solomon’s outpost in the waste, a city raised where there was no city, deep in the wilderness beyond Israel’s settled bounds: “And Baalath, and Tadmor in the wilderness, in the land” (1Ki 9:18). The Chronicler tells the same: “And he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities, which he built in Hamath” (2Ch 8:4). Here the peaceable kingdom of Solomon reached out its hand and planted rest and provision where before there was only sand and silence. The name means the place of palms, and a palm in the desert is a sign of water hidden and life sustained against all likelihood. That a king should build a walled and watered city in the trackless waste is a parable of dominion — the wilderness made to serve the throne, the barren place made fruitful by a wise ruler’s command. But Solomon in all his glory was a shadow, and the reach of his kingdom a faint drawing of a greater. The true Son of David has a dominion that runs to the ends of the earth, and He builds His city in wildernesses far darker than Tadmor’s. Where the gospel comes, the desert rejoices and blossoms as the rose; He plants His church in the waste places of the nations and makes the parched ground a pool. Tadmor in the wilderness whispers of the King whose dominion fills the earth.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Solomon’s far-reaching, peaceable kingdom was a shadow, and the substance is Christ. The greater Son of David asks of the Father and receives the uttermost parts of the earth for His possession; He plants His church in wildernesses darker than Tadmor’s, and where His gospel comes the desert blossoms as the rose. Look past the shadow to the King whose dominion fills the waste places of the world.

etymology: Hebrew Tel Aviv, “mound of the ear of corn” or “hill of the flood”; the settlement of the Judean captives by the river Chebar where Ezekiel dwelt among them.
biblical_def: Tel-abib was a settlement of the exiles by the river Chebar, one of the mounds of Babylon where the carried-away of Judah were planted far from Zion. It is named in a single unforgettable verse, when the prophet returned from the vision of the glory of God to sit among his afflicted people: “Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days” (Eze 3:15). Here is the tenderness of the prophetic office and, deeper still, a figure of the gospel. Ezekiel did not preach at a distance to the exiles; he came to them, dwelt where they dwelt, and sat where they sat, silent and overwhelmed for seven days, bearing in his own soul the weight of their captivity before ever he opened his mouth. The LORD would not leave His people comfortless in the strange land; He set His prophet in the midst of them, and His presence went with them into exile. So the greater Prophet came not to a throne but to a manger, and sat where we sit, taking our flesh, bearing our burden, entering our estrangement under the curse. The God who placed Ezekiel at Tel-abib is the God who is with His people in every Babylon, and who will bring them home.

etymology: Hebrew Kasiphya, a place of the Babylonian dispersion, perhaps “place of silver”; whence Ezra summoned Levites and Nethinim for the house of God.
biblical_def: Casiphia was a place of the dispersion, and Scripture remembers it for one holy errand. When Ezra mustered the returning remnant by the river of Ahava and looked over the company, he found among them not one of the sons of Levi, and no house of God can be raised or served without those whom the LORD has set apart to minister. So he sent to Casiphia: “And I sent them with commandment unto Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia…that they should bring unto us ministers for the house of our God” (Ezr 8:17). Out of that far settlement came Levites and Nethinim, servants of the sanctuary, to take their appointed places in the worship of the returning church. Here is a pattern the church must never forget. A remnant on the way home is not equipped for worship until the LORD provides ministers for His house; the ordinances He has commanded require the officers He has ordained. Ezra would not go up short-handed, offering God a worship stripped of the servants Scripture requires, for the God who commands the house also commands who shall serve in it. This is the regulative principle in the wilderness of exile: the church gathers not what pleases her, but what her Lord appoints. Casiphia sent her Levites, and the house of God was served according to the pattern. So still the King of the church raises up ministers and sends them where His people need them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship is regulated by the Lord who commands it, not shaped by the will of the worshipper. Ezra would not go up without the ministers Scripture required, for the God who ordains the house ordains who shall serve in it. So the King of the church still raises up and sends ministers, that His people may offer the pure offering His name deserves among the nations.

etymology: Hebrew Hena, a city of the region the Assyrian had conquered; named by the Rabshakeh in his taunt against Jerusalem, that no god had delivered these cities from his master’s hand.
biblical_def: Hena is a name flung out in a blasphemer’s boast. When the Rabshakeh of Assyria stood before the walls of Jerusalem, he numbered the fallen cities like trophies and mocked the God of Judah with them: “Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah? have they delivered Samaria out of mine hand?” (2Ki 18:34). The same names return in Sennacherib’s letter: “Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and Ivah?” (2Ki 19:13). The Assyrian’s reasoning was simple and profane: the idols of Hena did not save Hena, therefore the God of Jerusalem cannot save Jerusalem. But he had confounded the living God with the dead gods of the heathen, and that is the sin of every boaster who measures the Almighty by the impotence of idols. The gods of Hena were nothing, wood and stone that could not deliver their own city; but the LORD made the heavens, and He is not as the gods of the nations. Hezekiah spread the blasphemous letter before the LORD, and in one night the angel of the LORD smote the camp of Assyria. Hena stands forever as the boaster’s miscalculation: the God who was mocked among the idols of the conquered cities is the God who saves His own for His own name’s sake.

etymology: Hebrew Ivvah, a city conquered by Assyria, paired with Hena in the Rabshakeh’s taunt; possibly the Ava whence colonists were later brought into Samaria.
biblical_def: Ivah is the twin of Hena in the Assyrian’s blasphemy, a conquered city whose gods had failed, named again and again to press the taunt against Jerusalem: “Where are the gods of Hamath, and of Arpad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?” (2Ki 18:34). Isaiah records the same boast in Sennacherib’s letter: “Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?” (Isa 37:13). The conqueror rolled these names off his tongue as proofs that heaven itself was powerless before him. Yet what did his catalogue of ruined cities prove? Only that idols are idols, that the graven things of Ivah could no more save Ivah than a scarecrow saves a field. The Assyrian mocked with the very emptiness of the gods he had overthrown, never seeing that the LORD who made the heavens stands in a different order of being altogether from the deaf and dumb idols of the nations. He is God, and there is none else. So the boast that named Ivah became the occasion of the LORD’s glory, for He would deliver Zion, not for her righteousness, but for His own sake and for His servant David’s sake. Ivah teaches that the emptiness of false gods is no measure of the true; the God whom the proud number among the idols of the conquered is the God who saves His city and shatters the boaster.

etymology: Hebrew Sepharad, a far land of the dispersion whither the captivity of Jerusalem was carried; named once in Obadiah’s prophecy of the sure return.
biblical_def: Sepharad is a single word in Obadiah, and it carries the whole weight of exile and return. The prophet, foretelling the ruin of Edom and the restoration of Jacob, names the far place to which the captives of Jerusalem had been swept: “And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel shall possess that of the Canaanites, even unto Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad, shall possess the cities of the south” (Oba 1:20). Where Sepharad lay men have long disputed, but the point of the verse is not its latitude; it is that the LORD knows exactly where His scattered people are. However far the exile, however obscure the land, the covenant reaches them, and the word of promise runs to the very edge of their banishment. The captivity that is in Sepharad shall not rot there; it shall possess the cities of the south, restored to the inheritance the LORD swore to the fathers. Here is the sure return that undergirds every dispersion of the church. The LORD gathers His own from the north and the south, from the islands of the sea and the ends of the earth; not one of His sheep is lost in any far country. What He scatters in judgment He gathers in mercy, and the exile of His people is never their end. Sepharad, the farthest mound of the banishment, is already marked for homecoming.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of the homecoming. The captivity that is in Sepharad shall not perish there, but shall possess the cities of the south; the covenant runs to the edge of the exile and calls the banished home.
